| |

**I’m Warren Howell, Candidate for Harris County Judge and it’s TIME TO STOP the madness.**
Since my first day on the Campaign Trail, I set out to create a written plan-of-execution for Day 1 one the job. My leadership will bring INNOVATION and true leadership to Harris County Commissoners Court - something that has been sorely lacking for quite some time.
My opponent in this runoff has been part of the local bureacratic machine for 18 out of the past 25 years. He is another politician playing musical chairs - looking for his next opportunity to get back into the machine.
We don’t need more bureaucrats - we need **real-world solutions** and **disciplined leadership.**
Beaurocrats are great at pointing out problems that stir emotion, but the “fix” is always MORE of YOUR TAX DOLLARS. It seems that no matter how many of OUR tax dollars are thrown at a problem, we never truly seem to solve anything. They create the problem, stir the emotion and offer the fix that is never truly fixed. Over and over and over.
**This runoff is a choice between endless beaurocracy or a real business solutions.** Do we want another smooth-talking bureaucrat or do we NEED a business man with an actual business PLAN to turn the county around, and clean house - top to bottom?
My administration will bring Harris County into the 21st century with cutting edge technologies and solutions that will forever end the waste, fraud and Harris County cronyism.
**LOOK OUT! ‘CAUSE HERE I COME!**[**Please rush a donation TODAY.**](https://howellforharriscounty.us4.list-manage.com/track/click?u=ab8c3a643a45a6e2b06d8f050&id=833abc9ee7&e=7c92d84deb)**I’m Warren Howell and I AM the Disruptor.**

_We CAN lower taxes. We CAN eliminate property taxes for our seniors. _ _And we CAN have a surplus again!_

**SMALLER GOVERNMENT = BETTER GOVERNMENT**. See My full plan to _MAKE HARRIS COUNTY GREAT AGAIN_ on the campaign website. [ _**👉 www.howellforharriscounty.com.**_](https://howellforharriscounty.us4.list-manage.com/track/click?u=ab8c3a643a45a6e2b06d8f050&id=a6239d357b&e=7c92d84deb)

name: Patrick J. Murphy
subject: What the NFL Draft Teaches About Life’s Transitions
body:
[https://prod.cdn.everyaction.com/images/van/NGP/NGP25/1/106220/images/PJM_Logo.png]
Most NFL careers are over by age 26. What comes next depends on quality mentorship.
I was in Pittsburgh before the start of the NFL Draft.
NFL Draft Week is an event that turns its host city into a kind of theme park for football fans. The city is expecting 700,000 visitors [https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/draft/2026/04/23/pittsburgh-hosts-nfl-draft-live-updates-schedule-map--live/89740626007/] over the next three days, more than double Pittsburgh’s population. Technically I was one of them. But I wasn’t there for the draft itself.
I was invited by Split Social [https://spiltsocial.com/] (thanks to partners Patrick Klein, Genine Fallon, Corey Myers, and Joshua Meyers) to speak at their Business Hop LINEAGE event [https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7453054197618368513/] , a private gathering built to connect athletes, investors, operators, veterans and brand leaders. I was joined by Super Bowl champion Will Allen, Jim Rooney (author and son of the Steelers ownership family), former NFL running back and certified NFL transition coach Keith Elias, and Charlotte Heyward, Executive Director of the Cameron Heyward Foundation.
We talked about mentorship and transition -- specifically, what happens to young men when the sport that formed their entire identity suddenly disappears from their life.
The path to getting drafted is a miracle in itself.
Over a million kids play high school football in this country. About 7% [https://www.uolivet.edu/how-many-high-school-athletes-play-in-college/] play in college. Roughly 1.5% of those ever get drafted. The NFL Draft gets framed as an almost coronation-like ceremony welcoming the elite into a dream career. A young athlete walks across a stage, shakes the commissioner’s hand, puts on his new NFL team hat, and the world calls it the start of a promising career.
But for most, it is actually closer to an ending that leads to a very disorienting retirement. The average NFL career lasts about three years– usually before the age of 26. While the NFL minimum salary starts at $840k [https://www.profootballnetwork.com/nfl-salaries-what-is-the-lowest-you-can-make-in-the-nfl/] , for most players, it won’t be enough to sustain them for the decades that follow when their career ends.
The structure that organized their entire lives – coaches, schedules, locker rooms, their fixed identity – disappears almost overnight once their playing days are over. What fills that space is harder to prepare for: financial decisions with no playbook, family expectations that arrive all at once, and an identity built around something that no longer exists as it once did.
So while the draft is a professional milestone, it’s also a personal transition. And transitions, especially high-stakes ones, are where people either gain clarity or lose themselves.
[https://prod.cdn.everyaction.com/images/van/NGP/NGP25/1/106220/images/NFL%20Draft%20PJM.png]
Lately, I have been watching The Chosen on Amazon Prime, it's a historical drama about the life of Jesus. There’s a message in the show that I was thinking about in Pittsburgh, and it’s that Jesus was never just teaching the disciples, He was preparing them for the mission after He was gone.
His purpose was mentorship. Teaching the apostles how to carry the work forward without Him physically beside them. The foundation of the Catholic Church was built not only on faith, but on discipleship.
The lesson is timeless, regardless of faith tradition or how you apply it: a mentor’s job is not simply to hand someone a fish. It is to teach them how to fish.
At the event I spoke about how real leadership involves leading with love.
The best leaders do not lead through fear. They lead through consistency, presence, and the willingness to care enough to tell the truth, building trust through their actions.
Jim Rooney: Faith as Leadership
On the stage with me was Jim Rooney, one of Dan and Patricia Rooney’s nine children.
In Pittsburgh, the Rooneys are synonymous with the Steelers’ legacy.
They’ve owned that franchise since 1933 -- longer than most American institutions have existed in their current form. They are tied with the Patriots for most Super Bowl wins–6– and doing that in a mid-sized rust belt city makes their story all the more remarkable.
Jim Rooney spent decades working alongside his father; he started as a ball boy and grew up watching Dan run the franchise from the inside. He later helped manage relationships at the State Department during his father's tenure as U.S. Ambassador to Ireland in the Obama Administration, contributed to the development of the Rooney Rule -- the 2003 NFL policy Dan championed requiring teams to interview minority candidates for head coaching jobs, now widely adopted across corporate America -- and has since built his own career in leadership consulting. He wrote it all down in his book A Different Way to Win [https://www.amazon.com/dp/1733404910?tag=patrickjmurph-20] which captures the philosophy that shaped the Rooney family legacy.
Order here. [https://www.amazon.com/dp/1733404910?tag=patrickjmurph-20]
[https://prod.cdn.everyaction.com/images/van/NGP/NGP25/1/106220/images/Rooney.png]
Jim spoke passionately about faith and how that was core to his family’s life as an operating principle. His father attended church every morning because he believed leaders should not bring their worries to work - to be present to lead and not let outside pressures fall on the people they were responsible for leading.
You absorb the pressure so the people around you can work freely. That same philosophy followed his father Dan to Ireland, where he served as U.S. Ambassador, building relationships across lines of faith, politics, and business.
Legacy, Jim said, isn't power. It's responsibility.
Will Allen: Finding Purpose Beyond Football
Will Allen spent twelve years in the NFL as a safety, won a national championship at Ohio State, and earned a Super Bowl ring. He's also been building businesses since before he retired. On stage he had a very specific point of view about what mentorship actually looks like inside a locker room.
Steelers culture, he said, was built on veterans taking younger players under their wing -- even when those younger players were competing for the same roster spot. That's a harder thing to do than it sounds. It requires enough security in yourself that someone else's success doesn't feel like a threat. Will pointed to Ryan Clark as an example of that done right. When he snapped at younger players during off season practice, Clark stepped in. They're grown men, he said. You can't talk to them that way. Correction without humiliation was important to him.
Will also understood early that football was never supposed to be his one calling in life. It was a platform, not his entire identity.
While still playing, he was already preparing for life after football. Through private equity work, entrepreneurial ventures like Capital56, and his commitment to athlete financial education, he built a model for players who wanted more than short-term success.
He believed the goal was never just to earn money, but to understand how money works, how ownership creates freedom, and how disciplined decision-making creates generational impact.
That's the model he built and the one he was still articulating Wednesday night in Pittsburgh, two decades after his first NFL snap.
Keith Elias: Life After Football
Keith Elias is a former NFL running back, a Princeton graduate, an entrepreneur and an investor.
He now works as the NFL's transition coach, which means his entire professional life is built around the problem we were all there to discuss.
He described catching a kickoff on Monday Night Football in front of 50,000 fans, the specific physical sensation of that, the way the noise becomes something you feel in your chest. Then he said something most athletes won't admit out loud: that rush may never come back at that intensity. The crowd, the stakes, the singular focus of an entire team and stadium -- it's a hard thing to replace.
But he said it does come back in different ways. The moment your child is born. The deal you spent two years closing. The look on a young colleague’s face when something finally clicks. The adrenaline isn't gone. It just presents itself in new ways.
Through his work, he helps NFL players find their purpose and next chapter in life after their playing career is over.
While we’re on mentorship, I was back at the Wharton Business School helping teach, coach, and mentor students at one of my favorite events - the annual Pitch Competition. MBAs and one undergrad student had the courage to stand up in front of us investors pitching their business idea, then standing their fielding questions. It takes guts to put yourself out there in business - and life - but it’s hard not to be inspired by their eagerness and tenacity.
In many ways it demands the same lessons that are applied to the NFL - or to my fellow veterans - coaching and preparing them to thrive in the real world.
The moment you graduate - like these NFL players once done playing football, or our soldiers no longer jumping out of perfectly fine airplanes - signals a transition where the structure you once had disappears.
The best thing any of us can do for the people coming up behind us is to make sure we offered our hand when they needed it most. To give them the tools, the network and the coaching to continue excelling in their next mission as they find their purpose.
- Patrick
P.S. Thank you reading our newsletter. For more updates, please follow on Instagram [https://bit.ly/47s6mRv] and subscribe to my best-selling (31st in country) Substack [https://bit.ly/4te4VOV] for our weekly geopolitical and business analysis. Most importantly, please keep our troops and everyone in the region in your nightly prayers.

He now works as the NFL's transition coach, which means his entire professional life is built around the problem we were all there to discuss. He described catching a kickoff on Monday Night Football in front of 50,000 fans, the specific physical sensation of that, the way the noise becomes something you feel in your chest. Then he said something most athletes won't admit out loud: that rush may never come back at that intensity. The crowd, the stakes, the singular focus of an entire team and stadium -- it's a hard thing to replace. But he said it does come back in different ways. The moment your child is born. The deal you spent two years closing. The look on a young colleague’s face when something finally clicks. The adrenaline isn't gone. It just presents itself in new ways. Through his work, he helps NFL players find their purpose and next chapter in life after their playing career is over. While we’re on mentorship, I was back at the Wharton Business School helping teach, coach, and mentor students at one of my favorite events - the annual Pitch Competition. MBAs and one undergrad student had the courage to stand up in front of us investors pitching their business idea, then standing their fielding questions. It takes guts to put yourself out there in business - and life - but it’s hard not to be inspired by their eagerness and tenacity. In many ways it demands the same lessons that are applied to the NFL - or to my fellow veterans - coaching and preparing them to thrive in the real world. The moment you graduate - like these NFL players once done playing football, or our soldiers no longer jumping out of perfectly fine airplanes - signals a transition where the structure you once had disappears. The best thing any of us can do for the people coming up behind us is to make sure we offered our hand when they needed it most. To give them the tools, the network and the coaching to continue excelling in their next mission as they find their purpose. - Patrick P.S. Thank you reading our newsletter. body:
| I need to apologize to you.
I'm sorry, truly I am.
I'm sorry that some people accuse you of not being MAGA if you don't make a donation.
I'm sorry that some people lie to you about who they are to try to trick you into donating.
And I'm sorry that many folks don't even show their appreciation when you do donate.
It drives me crazy that people try to treat you like that, and it's important to hear why I do things differently.
First things first.
This is Majority Leader Steve Scalise.
Secondly, I want to thank you for all of the support you've given to the GOP over the years; it really means a lot.
But right now we're staring down some concerning numbers, and it has my team and I really worried.
The Democrats are currently unloading 100 million dollars into 35 GOP seats to obliterate our House Majority once and for all, and here is the truth: Right now, we simply don't have the funds to fully fund our campaign operations in all 35 races.
[So the simple truth is that I need your help before our House Majority is a thing of the past.](http://links.right-red.com/u/click?_t=7f2cc7f35be547959fee68a54bdac0d9&_m=7a123b1e55364bea8cada2fd1917bb19&_e=2ROsJAW-j59pDDafX0rKK1MrQbzp_dUky1K7ouN2GfnVbKyjmd6HKoIdbh_Y4XrxH0K4EdA9vN4Lb2AmfvOTtUWvYIUQx4M9SRiQSUklnFZ2x9BtxoC9FM2Tu37YloBGvokN_Ns1imhK-13qbh94Q4FdH8HMjxUFOFsvybX-mL1cPxDFE8NinzKNsgViOjvdeR61im26YD2UIKVYjJyOmCdu7OOsQJH4GmjWcxfg8g6an3sCN7oVIvsHpyjJxZKASDc6-LeRFIkZMvydLlhQUYXYmjB4-I8vi3IbfWxgkF8z9LWo6uhBCfaMDLI9vcgDpWTGKB_-UmCNNOLq9LYSf5GVzqz6B-pK7IRQU-mJt3YA1zQagWs7G4f8kyPOoYOrkDzoXKCqcC-wVAi8-hfH6Gczle1avan2Tqzzjh3QnRslpokmlznQovi8LaVMoEOsxPWb5VEdQgy1A4Egub_26qQ7JtcFe1oW0zVF34sT4FUDUNn2EOFOrel7y_A2lSBctGqCBKbYf02IUKRPFhIPg-lTyBkWiUDWxCMmu7pHBd6miwzhbXw9c4Q3u3fX_ndiJskQVcsZcXEfY3ZfADSFUdOSxKDOwKdW32YB0N_XUyHt3soJGjz3dDARAuP2IpqruGsdR35pCqhaEKD9HHy4nSMZmbZHzfHKeYuDp2uEk67rUUIFdunbIpOMiegc3759)

# **Trump calls for 2020 election to be "permanently wiped from the books" if SPLC convicted of fraud**
President Donald Trump demanded Friday that **[the 2020 election be erased](https://substack.com/redirect/90dd7a05-8696-42dc-bb66-a80524a8acdf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** if the Southern Poverty Law Center is convicted of wire fraud, bank fraud, and money laundering, writing on Truth Social "The Southern Poverty Law Center, one of the greatest political scams in American History, has been charged with FRAUD... If it is true, the 2020 Presidential Election should be permanently wiped from the books and be of no further force or effect!"
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/90dd7a05-8696-42dc-bb66-a80524a8acdf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **What SPLC is accused of** : The SPLC was indicted Tuesday with prosecutors alleging the group secretly funneled $3 million in donated funds to white supremacist groups--including the KKK, American Nazi Party, National Socialist Movement, and Unite the Right--between 2014 and 2023 while donors believed funds would "dismantle" such organizations. One Unite the Right leader received over $270,000 over eight years, while an informant identified as "F-9" was allegedly paid more than $1 million and stole 25 boxes of neo-Nazi documents, with another person paid $6,000 to falsely take responsibility for the theft.
* **SPLC claims political targeting** : SPLC CEO Bryan Fair claimed the group was being targeted for "prior use of paid confidential informants to gather credible intelligence on extremely violent groups," but Acting AG Todd Blanche told reporters the organization was not "dismantling these groups" but "instead manufacturing the extremism it purports to oppose by paying sources to stoke racial hatred." FBI Director Kash Patel severed the agency's relationship with SPLC in October, calling them "a partisan smear machine" whose "hate map" has "been used to defame mainstream Americans and even inspired violence."

# **SPLC urged Biden admin to release transgender immigrant convicted of sexually assaulting 14-year-old girl**
The Southern Poverty Law Center, now subject of a massive federal indictment, previously **[urged the Biden administration to release a transgender immigrant](https://substack.com/redirect/1c0425ad-e7dc-40f3-894b-0f58227baca9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** convicted of sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl, according to documents obtained by the Oversight Project via FOIA. **[In a 2021 email,](https://substack.com/redirect/a230ff1e-89e8-4ca2-b377-a6fc8b9e9d57?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** an SPLC attorney asked ICE to "release" the detainee "as soon as possible" due to "hypertension and severe anxiety," arguing the individual "does not fall within the administration's public safety enforcement priority" and citing trauma related to transgender identity.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/1c0425ad-e7dc-40f3-894b-0f58227baca9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **The crime** : The immigrant, a female who identifies as male, had served more than eight years for sexually assaulting the 14-year-old in 2011 when the perpetrator was 19 years old after a two-year online relationship. The transgender-identifying woman learned the girl had lied about her age and was just 14, but "proceeded with the meet-up where 'they engaged in sexual conduct.'" The SPLC attorney acknowledged the "conviction on its face appears grave" but argued for "additional context" including feelings of childhood isolation "with respect to his gender identity." A July 2021 Homeland Security email confirmed "career officials determined" the detainee "should be released" with a tracking device.
* **SPLC now under federal indictment** : A grand jury indicted the SPLC Tuesday on multiple fraud and money laundering counts, with the Justice Department alleging the group "secretly funneled more than $3 million in funds to white supremacist & extremist groups" including Aryan Nations and KKK members. Acting AG Todd Blanche said the SPLC was "manufacturing the extremism it purports to oppose by paying sources to stoke racial hatred."

I wanted to use some of that time to reach out, because I think it’s important that you know how much I appreciate your support.
#

Hey, it's Mark.
I’ve got a minute to spare right now. That might not sound like much, but with things as busy as they’ve been, I’ll take whatever I can get.
I wanted to use some of that time to reach out, because I think it’s important that you know how much I appreciate your support.
I’ve had some pretty cool jobs before, but never anything like this. The team we’ve built together numbers in the millions, and I can’t tell you how humbling that is. That you’re still here after everything that’s happened means the world to me.
The simple truth is that I could not do this without your support. I know I don’t say it enough, but thank you. Truly.
But today, I’m asking you to help me continue the momentum we’ve built over these last several months. We’ve put together a tremendous movement, and we have a big opportunity to translate that into results.
If you want to help me elect Democrats to the House and Senate and flip Congress, here’s how you can do it:

clean_body: Trump wants to disenfranchise these communities | = Peter, Donald Trump is so scared about what could happen in November’s midterm elections that he’s trying everything he can to keep Americans from the ballot box. He targeted mail-in voting with unconstitutional executive orders. He pressured House Republicans to pass a bill that would disenfranchise millions of women and LGBTQ+ Americans. And now, he’s backing a Supreme Court lawsuit that could bar states from counting ballots that arrive after Election Day — even if they were mailed on time. Thousands of Americans in rural communities rely on those ballots being counted. ******=**** | = The Supreme Court appears ready to side with Trump and invalidate ballots received after Election Day, regardless of when they were postmarked. That would have huge consequences in states with must-win U.S. House races like Arizona: more than 80% of Arizonans vote by mail, and they’ve safely done so for decades. A ruling in Trump’s favor could make it harder for voters in rural communities across more than a dozen critical states to have their ballots counted — and that’s exactly the point. Derek, I am all in on this election — and I hope you are too. Here at Campaign HQ, we’ve been working around the clock to get our message out across the Commonwealth through campaign events, social media, and yes, emails like these. We’re meeting folks where they are, and we’re _listening_ to them... not just talking to them. That’s the difference between our campaign and our opponent’s, Derek. My opponent is more than happy to rattle off the President’s talking points — but when it comes time to answer the tough questions? Silence. [_**We’ve already reached thousands of Pennsylvanians since Launch Day — but there’s still so much work left on our plate. Please, will you chip in to help our campaign reach, persuade, and turn out millions of Pennsylvanians? I was in Pittsburgh before the start of the NFL Draft.
NFL Draft Week is an event that turns its host city into a kind of theme park for football fans. The city is expecting [700,000 visitors](https://substack.com/redirect/5f6fc071-e102-411a-811a-e832f01d31ef?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) over the next three days, more than double Pittsburgh's population. Technically, I was one of them. But I wasn't there for the draft itself.
I was invited by [Split Social ](https://substack.com/redirect/4a21cf52-9e0c-44e5-a32d-f0e5e039d4af?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)(thanks to partners Patrick Klein, Genine Fallon, Corey Myers, and Joshua Meyers) to speak at their [Business Hop LINEAGE event](https://substack.com/redirect/d14ad603-15e9-42b0-9ea1-9e23b2fab68e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), a private gathering built to connect athletes, investors, operators, veterans, and brand leaders.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/be2f0574-393b-44f6-8fc3-c6cacb029e01?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
I was joined by Super Bowl champion Will Allen, Jim Rooney (author and son of the Steelers ownership family), former NFL running back and certified NFL transition coach Keith Elias, and Charlotte Heyward-Wesley, Executive Director of the Cameron Heyward Foundation.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/d25bd67b-71bb-409a-ab45-f6d5e0f9690b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Pictured (left to right): Charlotte Heyward-Wesley, Kevin Marginian, Josiah Myers, Keith Elias, Genine Fallon, Patrick Murphy, Patrick Klein
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/e3b22189-460d-4679-8eaf-845ea3ebe87a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Wayne Allen, Patrick Murphy, Jim Rooney.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/e19e41cc-a98c-4e68-8385-51464692e3d9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
We talked about mentorship and transition - specifically, what happens to young men when the sport that formed their entire identity suddenly disappears from their lives.
The path to getting drafted is a miracle in itself.
Over a million kids play high school football in this country. About [7%](https://substack.com/redirect/2efad911-a648-4ce9-a3b5-9c87872e12b9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) play in college. Roughly 1.5% of those ever get drafted. The NFL Draft gets framed as an almost coronation-like ceremony welcoming the elite into a dream career. A young athlete walks across a stage, shakes the commissioner's hand, puts on his new NFL team hat, and the world calls it the start of a promising career.
But for most, it is actually closer to an ending that leads to a very disorienting retirement. The average NFL career lasts about three years - usually before the age of 26. While the NFL minimum salary starts at [$840k](https://substack.com/redirect/c8b925b8-60f9-4365-8be0-e98dba60296f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), for most players, it won't be enough to sustain them for the decades that follow when their career ends.
The structure that organized their entire lives - coaches, schedules, locker rooms, their fixed identity - disappears almost overnight once their playing days are over. What fills that space is harder to prepare for: financial decisions with no playbook, family expectations that arrive all at once, and an identity built around something that no longer exists as it once did.
So while the draft is a professional milestone, it's also a personal transition. And transitions, especially high-stakes ones, are where people either gain clarity or lose themselves.
Lately, I have been watching _The Chosen_ on Amazon Prime, it's a historical drama about the life of Jesus. There's a message in the show that I was thinking about in Pittsburgh, and it's that Jesus was never just teaching the disciples, He was preparing them for the mission after He was gone.
His purpose was mentorship. Teaching the apostles how to carry the work forward without Him physically beside them. The foundation of the Catholic Church was built not only on faith, but on discipleship.
The lesson is timeless, regardless of faith tradition or how you apply it: a mentor's job is not simply to hand someone a fish. It is to teach them how to fish.
At the event, I spoke about how real leadership involves leading with love.
The best leaders do not lead through fear. They lead through consistency, presence, and the willingness to care enough to tell the truth, building trust through their actions.

## **Jim Rooney: Faith as Leadership**
On the stage with me was Jim Rooney, one of Dan and Patricia Rooney's nine children.
In Pittsburgh, the Rooneys are synonymous with the Steelers' legacy.
They've owned that franchise since 1933 - longer than most American institutions have existed in their current form. They are tied with the Patriots for most Super Bowl wins -6- and doing that in a mid-sized rust belt city makes their story all the more remarkable.
Jim Rooney spent decades working alongside his father; he started as a ball boy and grew up watching Dan run the franchise from the inside. He later helped manage relationships at the State Department during his father's tenure as U.S. Ambassador to Ireland in the Obama Administration, contributed to the development of the Rooney Rule - the 2003 NFL policy Dan championed requiring teams to interview minority candidates for head coaching jobs, now widely adopted across corporate America -and has since built his own career in leadership consulting. He wrote it all down in his book _[A Different Way to Win](https://substack.com/redirect/01010d5f-0b13-42d6-859c-22c0ec7fe8ed?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) ,_ which captures the philosophy that shaped the Rooney family legacy.
[Order here.](https://substack.com/redirect/01010d5f-0b13-42d6-859c-22c0ec7fe8ed?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/cb41adaf-6353-4dde-abf0-83ee5f2b1840?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Jim spoke passionately about faith and how that was core to his family's life as an operating principle. His father attended church every morning because he believed leaders should not bring their worries to work - to be present to lead and not let outside pressures fall on the people they were responsible for leading.
You absorb the pressure so the people around you can work freely. That same philosophy followed his father, Dan, to Ireland, where he served as U.S. Ambassador, building relationships across lines of faith, politics, and business.
Legacy, Jim said, isn't power. It's responsibility.
## **Will Allen: Finding Purpose Beyond Football**
Will Allen spent twelve years in the NFL as a safety, won a national championship at Ohio State, and earned a Super Bowl ring. He's also been building businesses since before he retired. On stage, he had a very specific point of view about what mentorship actually looks like inside a locker room.
Steelers culture, he said, was built on veterans taking younger players under their wing - even when those younger players were competing for the same roster spot. That's a harder thing to do than it sounds. It requires enough security in yourself that someone else's success doesn't feel like a threat. Will pointed to Ryan Clark as an example of that done right. When he snapped at younger players during off-season practice, Clark stepped in. They're grown men, he said. You can't talk to them that way. Correction without humiliation was important to him.
Will also understood early that football was never supposed to be his one calling in life. It was a platform, not his entire identity.
While still playing, he was already preparing for life after football. Through private equity work, entrepreneurial ventures like Capital56, and his commitment to athlete financial education, he built a model for players who wanted more than short-term success.
He believed the goal was never just to earn money, but to understand how money works, how ownership creates freedom, and how disciplined decision-making creates generational impact.
That's the model he built and the one he was still articulating Wednesday night in Pittsburgh, two decades after his first NFL snap.
## **Keith Elias: Life After Football**
Keith Elias is a former NFL running back, a Princeton graduate, an entrepreneur, and an investor.
He now works as the NFL's transition coach, which means his entire professional life is built around the problem we were all there to discuss.
He described catching a kickoff on Monday Night Football in front of 50,000 fans, the specific physical sensation of that, the way the noise becomes something you feel in your chest. Then he said something most athletes won't admit out loud: that rush may never come back at that intensity. The crowd, the stakes, the singular focus of an entire team and stadium -- it's a hard thing to replace.
But he said it does come back in different ways. The moment your child is born. The deal you spent two years closing. The look on a young colleague's face when something finally clicks. The adrenaline isn't gone. It just presents itself in new ways.
Through his work, he helps NFL players find their purpose and next chapter in life after their playing career is over.
***
While we're on mentorship, I was back at the Wharton Business School helping teach, coach, and mentor students at one of my favorite events - the annual Pitch Competition. MBAs and one undergrad student had the courage to stand up in front of us investors, pitching their business idea, then holding their ground, fielding questions. It takes guts to put yourself out there in business - and in life - but it's hard not to be inspired by their eagerness and tenacity.
In many ways, it demands the same lessons that are applied to the NFL - or to my fellow veterans - coaching and preparing them to thrive in the real world.
The moment you graduate - like these NFL players once done playing football, or our soldiers no longer jumping out of perfectly fine airplanes - signals a transition where the structure you once had disappears.
The best thing any of us can do for the people coming up behind us is to make sure we offer our hand when they need it most. To give them the tools, the network, and the coaching to continue excelling in their next mission as they find their purpose.

NFL Draft Week is an event that turns its host city into a kind of theme park for football fans. The city is expecting over the next three days, more than double Pittsburgh's population. Technically, I was one of them. But I wasn't there for the draft itself. I was invited by to partners Patrick Klein, Genine Fallon, Corey Myers, and Joshua Meyers) to speak at their , a private gathering built to connect athletes, investors, operators, veterans, and brand leaders. | | ---|---|--- I was joined by Super Bowl champion Will Allen, Jim Rooney (author and son of the Steelers ownership family), former NFL running back and certified NFL transition coach Keith Elias, and Charlotte Heyward-Wesley, Executive Director of the Cameron Heyward Foundation. | | ---|---|--- Pictured (left to right): Charlotte Heyward-Wesley, Kevin Marginian, Josiah Myers, Keith Elias, Genine Fallon, Patrick Murphy, Patrick Klein | | ---|---|--- Wayne Allen, Patrick Murphy, Jim Rooney. | | ---|---|--- We talked about mentorship and transition - specifically, what happens to young men when the sport that formed their entire identity suddenly disappears from their lives. The path to getting drafted is a miracle in itself. Over a million kids play high school football in this country. About play in college. Roughly 1.5% of those ever get drafted. The NFL Draft gets framed as an almost coronation-like ceremony welcoming the elite into a dream career. A young athlete walks across a stage, shakes the commissioner's hand, puts on his new NFL team hat, and the world calls it the start of a promising career. But for most, it is actually closer to an ending that leads to a very disorienting retirement. The average NFL career lasts about three years - usually before the age of 26. While the NFL minimum salary starts at , for most players, it won't be enough to sustain them for the decades that follow when their career ends. The structure that organized their entire lives - coaches, schedules, locker rooms, their fixed identity - disappears almost overnight once their playing days are over. What fills that space is harder to prepare for: financial decisions with no playbook, family expectations that arrive all at once, and an identity built around something that no longer exists as it once did. So while the draft is a professional milestone, it's also a personal transition. And transitions, especially high-stakes ones, are where people either gain clarity or lose themselves. Lately, I have been watching The Chosen on Amazon Prime, it's a historical drama about the life of Jesus. There's a message in the show that I was thinking about in Pittsburgh, and it's that Jesus was never just teaching the disciples, He was preparing them for the mission after He was gone. His purpose was mentorship. Teaching the apostles how to carry the work forward without Him physically beside them. The foundation of the Catholic Church was built not only on faith, but on discipleship. The lesson is timeless, regardless of faith tradition or how you apply it: a mentor's job is not simply to hand someone a fish. It is to teach them how to fish. At the event, I spoke about how real leadership involves leading with love. The best leaders do not lead through fear. They lead through consistency, presence, and the willingness to care enough to tell the truth, building trust through their actions. The Secretary's SitRep is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Jim Rooney: Faith as Leadership On the stage with me was Jim Rooney, one of Dan and Patricia Rooney's nine children. In Pittsburgh, the Rooneys are synonymous with the Steelers' legacy. They've owned that franchise since 1933 - longer than most American institutions have existed in their current form. They are tied with the Patriots for most Super Bowl wins -6- and doing that in a mid-sized rust belt city makes their story all the more remarkable. Jim Rooney spent decades working alongside his father; he started as a ball boy and grew up watching Dan run the franchise from the inside. He later helped manage relationships at the State Department during his father's tenure as U.S. Ambassador to Ireland in the Obama Administration, contributed to the development of the Rooney Rule - the 2003 NFL policy Dan championed requiring teams to interview minority candidates for head coaching jobs, now widely adopted across corporate America -and has since built his own career in leadership consulting. He wrote it all down in his book , which captures the philosophy that shaped the Rooney family legacy. | | ---|---|--- Jim spoke passionately about faith and how that was core to his family's life as an operating principle. His father attended church every morning because he believed leaders should not bring their worries to work - to be present to lead and not let outside pressures fall on the people they were responsible for leading. You absorb the pressure so the people around you can work freely. That same philosophy followed his father, Dan, to Ireland, where he served as U.S. Ambassador, building relationships across lines of faith, politics, and business. Legacy, Jim said, isn't power. It's responsibility. Will Allen: Finding Purpose Beyond Football Will Allen spent twelve years in the NFL as a safety, won a national championship at Ohio State, and earned a Super Bowl ring. He's also been building businesses since before he retired. On stage, he had a very specific point of view about what mentorship actually looks like inside a locker room. Steelers culture, he said, was built on veterans taking younger players under their wing - even when those younger players were competing for the same roster spot. That's a harder thing to do than it sounds. It requires enough security in yourself that someone else's success doesn't feel like a threat. Will pointed to Ryan Clark as an example of that done right. When he snapped at younger players during off-season practice, Clark stepped in. They're grown men, he said. You can't talk to them that way. Correction without humiliation was important to him. Will also understood early that football was never supposed to be his one calling in life. It was a platform, not his entire identity. While still playing, he was already preparing for life after football. Through private equity work, entrepreneurial ventures like Capital56, and his commitment to athlete financial education, he built a model for players who wanted more than short-term success. He believed the goal was never just to earn money, but to understand how money works, how ownership creates freedom, and how disciplined decision-making creates generational impact. That's the model he built and the one he was still articulating Wednesday night in Pittsburgh, two decades after his first NFL snap. Keith Elias: Life After Football Keith Elias is a former NFL running back, a Princeton graduate, an entrepreneur, and an investor. He now works as the NFL's transition coach, which means his entire professional life is built around the problem we were all there to discuss. He described catching a kickoff on Monday Night Football in front of 50,000 fans, the specific physical sensation of that, the way the noise becomes something you feel in your chest. Then he said something most athletes won't admit out loud: that rush may never come back at that intensity. The crowd, the stakes, the singular focus of an entire team and stadium -- it's a hard thing to replace. But he said it does come back in different ways. The moment your child is born. The deal you spent two years closing. The look on a young colleague's face when something finally clicks. The adrenaline isn't gone. It just presents itself in new ways. Through his work, he helps NFL players find their purpose and next chapter in life after their playing career is over. * While we're on mentorship, I was back at the Wharton Business School helping teach, coach, and mentor students at one of my favorite events - the annual Pitch Competition. MBAs and one undergrad student had the courage to stand up in front of us investors, pitching their business idea, then holding their ground, fielding questions. It takes guts to put yourself out there in business - and in life - but it's hard not to be inspired by their eagerness and tenacity. In many ways, it demands the same lessons that are applied to the NFL - or to my fellow veterans - coaching and preparing them to thrive in the real world. The moment you graduate - like these NFL players once done playing football, or our soldiers no longer jumping out of perfectly fine airplanes - signals a transition where the structure you once had disappears. The best thing any of us can do for the people coming up behind us is to make sure we offer our hand when they need it most. To give them the tools, the network, and the coaching to continue excelling in their next mission as they find their purpose. The Secretary's SitRep is a reader-supported publication. Peter,

One thing I hear a lot while I'm meeting people in SE Iowa is a lot of worry from our local farmers. They know that keeping up the farm and preventing a takeover by outside interests is going to take the next generation stepping up. **But Miller-Meeks' policies are discouraging young people from keeping the family legacy going with high costs, trade wars, and uncertainty.**

I know this story all too well. My grandparents had a family farm. They looked forward to the day when my dad would take it over and continue to build on the family's generations of hard work. But their costs were high, profits were low, and then the government used eminent domain to cut an interstate through their property, splitting the farm apart and making it harder to access.

The way of life they loved became unsustainable, so my dad had to quit school at just 16 years old and get another job to help the family get by. His future changed, and so did the farm's.

**Now, farming families in Iowa are facing the same dilemma.** Mariannette Miller-Meeks' reckless tariffs, big ag consolidation, and a lack of competition are driving up costs, while trade wars are taking away markets farmers could once rely on. To make things worse, the USDA just cut funding to an Eastern Iowa program that provides training for new farmers and helps them with the financial side of farming.

We need to protect family farms and make sure they have the resources to continue thriving long after we're gone. In Congress, I will work to make sure our farms receive the support they need to be successful, and that our future farmers have a legacy to continue.

clean_body: | = Peter, One thing I hear a lot while I'm meeting people in SE Iowa is a lot of worry from our local farmers. They know that keeping up the farm and preventing a takeover by outside interests is going to take the next generation stepping up. But Miller-Meeks' policies are discouraging young people from keeping the family legacy going with high costs, trade wars, and uncertainty. I know this story all too well. My grandparents had a family farm. They looked forward to the day when my dad would take it over and continue to build on the family's generations of hard work. But their costs were high, profits were low, and then the government used eminent domain to cut an interstate through their property, splitting the farm apart and making it harder to access. The way of life they loved became unsustainable, so my dad had to quit school at just 16 years old and get another job to help the family get by. His future changed, and so did the farm's. Now, farming families in Iowa are facing the same dilemma. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' reckless tariffs, big ag consolidation, and a lack of competition are driving up costs, while trade wars are taking away markets farmers could once rely on. To make things worse, the USDA just cut funding to an Eastern Iowa program that provides training for new farmers and helps them with the financial side of farming. We need to protect family farms and make sure they have the resources to continue thriving long after we're gone. Voter Action Project [https://voteractionproject.org/]
NC Newsline: Amid protests, NC elections board rejects campus voting sites and Sunday voting in several counties [http://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-power?refcode=042426_1&amount=25]
We're facing the repercussions of the partisan election takeover laws that went into effect at the end of 2024, Team.
To refresh your memory: After the 2024 elections and the defeat of a MAGA candidate for governor, opponents of voting rights in North Carolina jammed through a bill that took the power of the governor to appoint people to election boards and handed that to the state auditor . It's worth noting that the state auditor is the only statewide elected Republican, with Democrats winning the 2024 races for governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, and secretary of state.
Now, among massive protests from young voters, the MAGA-fied North Carolina State Elections Board recently shot down proposals to continue having early voting sites at several universities around the state . These weren't new sites either; these were places where North Carolina had provided early voting locations for a decade or more.
This is voter suppression, plain and simple, by making it harder for eligible, registered voters to vote in-person by taking away their polling place. It's another demonstration of how opponents of voting rights in North Carolina are more focused on expanding and cementing their own power than they are in serving the people and having fair elections.
We have to fight these suppressive actions in North Carolina and any other state where opponents of voting rights try to replicate this. Step up with $35 or whatever you can today to help every eligible voter cast their ballot >> [http://secure.actblue.com/donate/ifvap-power?refcode=042426_1&amount=35]

These new, highly partisan State Election Board members wouldn't even look the protestors in the eye or engage with their proposals. After the vote, Chairman Francis De Luca threatened to call the cops on students if they didn’t leave.
Need to better understand how this impacts young voters? Western Carolina University in Jackson County, for example, has had a polling place on campus since 2016 that’s been used in five general elections and four primaries, according to a document prepared for the board. The state board voted 3-2 to get rid of it.
Closing the campus voting site would not save money, but “ would create barriers to voting for young, rural residents ,” Jackson County Board member Betsy Swift told the state board. 64% of students don’t have vehicles to drive to the polling place, she said.
Without the on-campus site, the closest polling place for students will be a recreation center nearly two miles away. Students without transportation will have to walk along a four-lane highway and through a meadow to get there.
Voter suppression isn't just black and white photos of eligible voters being turned away from polling places. Voter suppression is making it harder for eligible voters to take part in our elections through onerous ID requirements, closing polling places, taking away voting locations, or ending mail-in voting. Every time someone makes it harder to cast your ballot, voters are suppressed.
It's not going to end until we stop them.

The _Social Determinants for Moms Act_ will:
* Address non-medical factors like housing, nutrition, and transportation that affect maternal outcomes.
* Establish a task force at HHS to coordinate data and accountability across agencies.
* Provide grants to trusted community organizations so they can deliver targeted support to pregnant and postpartum people where they live.

Research makes it clear that clinical care alone is not enough — social conditions drive disparities in maternal health.
**We cannot settle for a system that leaves communities behind.**

Friend, it's not your imagination: **Trump has it out for Colorado.**
Since he took office, he and his administration have:
❌ Moved the Space Command HQ from Colorado Springs to Alabama

❌ Gutted over $1 BILLION in grants for clean energy and public health

❌ Dismantled the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder

❌ Demanded we hand over sensitive voter information without justification

❌ **And last week, FEMA rejected our request for assistance following last year’s Elk and Lee Fires.**

name: April McClain Delaney for Congress Volunteer Team
subject: McClain Delaney Weekly Volunteer Round-Up
disclaimer_text: PAID FOR BY APRIL MCCLAIN DELANEY FOR CONGRESS
body:
https://www.everyaction.com/ [https://www.everyaction.com/]
Weekly Montgomery
Volunteer Round-Up
60 Days Until the Primary Election
This weekly email highlights all local events, canvassing, and phone bank opportunities!
Thank you for being what makes this campaign special. We hope to see you at all of the events below!
image of ... [https://prod.cdn.everyaction.com/images/van/NGP/NGP59/1/109172/images/4.29.24%20newsletter/IMG_9506%20%281%29_2.jpg]
Montgomery County Meet and Greet
Saturday, May 2nd, 3 PM - 5 PM
You are invited to an intimate Meet and Greet with Congresswoman April McClain Delaney and Montgomery County Council Members Dawn Luedtke, Marilyn Balcombe, and Kate Stewart.
Join us for an evening of meaningful conversation with the women who are working every day to strengthen our communities, deliver results for Maryland families, and build a future we can all be proud of.
Hosted graciously by JaLynn Prince, this is a rare opportunity to connect directly with your elected representatives in a comfortable, personal setting.
Sign Up Here [https://www.mobilize.us/aprilmcclaindelaneyforcongress/event/938012/]
Door Knocking
Saturday, May 2nd, 10 AM - 12 PM
Before you head to the Meet and Greet, help knock doors around Gaithersburg! We'll be heading out to engage with voters, share the positive work happening in our district, and get people excited to re-elect Congresswoman April McClain Delaney.
Whether you have canvassed 1000 times or 0 times, this is a great chance to get involved with the campaign! We will begin with a quick training session before heading out, and go out in pairs; no experience is necessary!
Bring comfortable shoes, water, and whatever attire the weather dictates! It'll be a great day of conversation and community as we work towards re-electing Congresswoman Delaney. We can't wait to see you there!
Sign Up Here [https://www.mobilize.us/aprilmcclaindelaneyforcongress/event/941157/]
(Virtual) Phone Banks
Thursday Night Phone Banks Sign Up [https://www.mobilize.us/aprilmcclaindelaneyforcongress/event/934939/]
Every Thursday night, 6-8 PM , until Election Night, we will have a virtual and in-person phone bank to turn out supporters and recruit more volunteers!
Either come on into the office or join from the comfort of your own home .
All you need is a phone and the willingness to make some calls. Hope to see you there!
Tuesday Night Phone Banks Sign Up [https://www.mobilize.us/aprilmcclaindelaneyforcongress/event/936896/]
Every Tuesday night, 6-8 PM, until Election Night, we will have a virtual phone bank, with an in-person option in Frederick coming soon. Help turn out supporters and grow our volunteer base!
Join from the comfort of your own home.
Gaithersburg Office Volunteering
Tuesday - Friday, 10 AM - 6 PM, Every Week
Join us at the campaign office to help re-elect Congresswoman April McClain Delaney! Our office is open Tuesday - Friday from 10 AM to 6 PM, and volunteers can jump in however they’d like—whether that’s knocking doors, making phone calls, or helping with important office projects that keep the campaign running.
You’re welcome to pop in for an hour or stay longer, whatever fits your schedule. We just ask that you sign up ahead of time so we can make sure we have materials, lists, and snacks ready for you. It’s a great way to meet fellow supporters, build community, and make a real impact in the campaign .
Sign Up Here [https://www.mobilize.us/aprilmcclaindelaneyforcongress/event/942348/]
Donations
Help Power This Campaign Donation Photo [https://prod.cdn.everyaction.com/images/van/NGP/NGP59/1/109172/images/4.14.24%20newsletter/IMG_9151%202%20%283%29.jpg]
We need your support to re-elect April to Congress! Any donation makes a world of difference.
Chip in Today [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/delaney-website?refcode=main-donate-link]
Best Regards, [https://prod.cdn.everyaction.com/images/van/NGP/NGP59/1/109172/images/IMG_0045.jpeg]
Gus Schmoll
Organizing Director

name: Tim Walz
subject: It’s not about wearing Carhartt and changing your own oil.
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Small Town PAC, [smalltownpac
body:
We don’t want to win just to win; we want to win to enact policies that improve people’s lives.
#
Peter,
On Day 1 of launching Small Town PAC, I went on MS NOW to spread the word and talk about why we need to build the infrastructure to elect more Democrats in rural communities across the country.
[](https://act.timwalz.com/go/73?c0=stp-ms-em-20260424-1.V5lZv1&amount=5&refcode=em20260424-522&t=1&akid=522%2E34582%2EE_W14p)
When I first ran for office, I was a 40-year-old school teacher who had absolutely zero political experience. I never attended a rally. I never attended a caucus. I voted, and that was **about it.**
**There are people out there who I know should be in Congress, who should be mayor, who should be vice presidential candidates.** _But they won’t if the infrastructure is not there._
In Minnesota, I had the advantage that people like the late Senator Paul Wellstone built organizations like Wellstone Action that took and trained me. They put a screen door in the middle of an auditorium on a Saturday, and had us knock on it and practice how to door-knock and talk to people.
We need to build more of that infrastructure and organization.
And it can’t be about holding power for the sake of holding power: it has to be about passing things like universal healthcare and strong public schools. We don’t want to win _just to win_ ; we want to win to enact policies that improve people’s lives.
**Reaching folks in small towns is not about wearing Carhartt and changing your own oil. It’s about understanding the angst that people are feeling, and fighting to pass policies that improve this country in a real, tangible way.**
**[That’s what Small Town PAC is all about. If you’re with me, pitch in $5 or whatever you can afford to get our movement off the ground.](https://act.timwalz.com/go/73?c0=stp-ms-em-20260424-1.V5lZv1&amount=5&refcode=em20260424-522&t=2&akid=522%2E34582%2EE_W14p)**
**[Donate $5 ››](https://act.timwalz.com/go/73?c0=stp-ms-em-20260424-1.V5lZv1&amount=5&refcode=20260424-522&t=21&akid=522%2E34582%2EE_W14p)**
With gratitude,
Tim

Tim Walz started Small Town PAC to build a Democratic Party that invests in small towns and delivers a message that resonates with rural America.
Together, we're finding and recruiting thoughtful, hardworking people to run for office, and supporting a new generation of leaders who truly reflect and understand their communities.
**[It’s time for Democrats to expand the map and put small towns back at the forefront: pitch in now to help build our movement from the ground up.](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/stp-ms-em-footer?refcode=em20260424-522&t=22&refcode2=522_34582_E_W14p&akid=522%2E34582%2EE_W14p)**
**[Donate](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/stp-ms-em-footer?refcode=em20260424-522-&t=23&refcode2=522_34582_E_W14p&akid=522%2E34582%2EE_W14p)**
This email was sent to dpwillis67@gmail.com. Email is the most important way we keep in touch with people like you, so thank you for reading to the end.

name: Forward Party
subject: Virginia’s Results Show What’s Broken and Why It Has to Change
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Forward Party and not authorized by any candidate or candidate's committee
body:
The real problem is not one party. It is the system itself. What is happening in Virginia reflects a broader cycle where redistricting is used to protect incumbents and lock in advantage.

| | | [ ](www.forwardparty.com)
---
### Peter —
Just a few years ago, Virginia voters took an important step toward fairer elections. In 2020, they approved a redistricting reform that created a bipartisan citizen-legislator commission to draw political maps, with the goal of reducing partisan influence and increasing transparency. Tuesday’s election results show how fragile that progress can be. Voters approved a new measure that will once again change how congressional maps are drawn in Virginia ahead of the 2026 election. That opens the door for lawmakers to redraw district lines in ways that could significantly reshape the state’s congressional delegation. Some projections suggest the current 6–5 split could shift dramatically, with Democrats potentially holding as many as 10 of Virginia’s 11 seats. Those kinds of outcomes are driven by how the lines are drawn. In some scenarios, densely populated urban and suburban areas in Northern Virginia could be combined with more rural regions in western and southwestern parts of the state, diluting competitive districts and making results more predictable. We have seen this pattern before. In states like Texas, Republicans have drawn maps that strongly favor their party, locking in advantages for years at a time. Moves like this have led Democrats in other states to respond in kind, creating a cycle where each side redraws maps to counter the other rather than competing for voters. At Forward, we oppose that, no matter who is doing it. **At the same time, it is important to acknowledge that not all of these situations are identical. In states like Virginia and California, voters were consulted and approved these changes. While we respectfully disagree with the outcome, we recognize that this approach is meaningfully different from situations in states like Texas, where maps have been imposed without that same level of voter input.** The real problem is not one party. It is the system itself. What is happening in Virginia reflects a broader cycle where redistricting is used to protect incumbents and lock in advantage. The result is a system with far too little competition. In recent election cycles, only about 30 to 40 out of 435 U.S. House races are considered truly competitive. Most districts are effectively safe seats where one party is overwhelmingly favored, and incumbents rarely lose, with reelection rates typically above 90 percent. When elections are not competitive, accountability breaks down. And voters are noticing. According to the latest Gallup poll released this week, just 10 percent of Americans approve of Congress, while 86 percent disapprove, **the lowest approval rating Gallup has ever recorded.** This is not a coincidence. When politicians pick their voters, general elections become predictable, independent voices struggle to compete, and incentives shift toward appealing to a narrow base instead of the broader public. That is not a healthy democracy. It is a closed system. Forward has been clear from the beginning. We oppose partisan gerrymandering by anyone, anywhere. It does not matter whether it benefits Democrats in Virginia or Republicans in another state. The outcome is the same. Voters are left with fewer choices and a system that becomes less representative over time. That is why we support independent redistricting commissions that put voters first. A better system would create more competitive districts, encourage candidates to speak to a broader range of voters, and reward problem solving instead of partisanship. Virginia’s result is a reminder of what is at stake. Voters should choose their representatives. Elections should be competitive. Politicians should have to earn support, not engineer it. **Please forward this to your friends, family, and coworkers. It helps us introduce them to Forward and to what we are building. Also consider inviting them to one of our upcoming events listed below. We'd love to meet them.**

From closed primaries to limited ballot access, the episode breaks down how the current structure favors party insiders while leaving everyday voters on the outside. We hope you enjoy! Don't forget to let us know what you think. Click the image below to watch. ICYMI: May is AAPI Heritage Month Join us as we officially launch the AAPI Committee on May 20th.We will be joined by Andrew Yang and other special guests For more information and to RSVP, click . If you’re tired of waiting for the system to fix itself — this is your moment.** 👥| 🗳️ | 💸 | 🌐 Contrary to what our detractors on social media say, YES, we read! As political divisions deepen across the United States, more Americans than ever are looking for an alternative to the traditional two-party system. One group prioritizing local races and running candidates in the Grand Strand believes it has the answer. Nationally organized in 2021 by Democratic former presidential candidate Andrew Yang and Republican former New Jersey Governor and EPA Administrator Christine Todd Whitman, the Forward Party is recognized on ballots in six states, including South Carolina. Op-Ed: (possible paywall) In Arizona, the two legacy political parties are in a panic. From the intensity of their response, you would think the recently renamed (AIP), with a modest footprint and a broad vision, represents an existential threat. The reaction was so strong that Democrats and Republicans banded together to prevent the AIP’s name change from the No Labels Party of Arizona. Copyright © 2026 Forward Party, all rights reserved. | | Friend, Welcome to the latest edition of Sarah Explains It All. My goal for this series is to cut through the political spin and give you the unvarnished facts about how policy in Washington is actually impacting our lives. Today, we need to talk about a single, sobering number: **190,000** A new analysis revealed that **as many as 190,000 Marylanders are at risk of losing their Medicaid coverage under the Trump Administration’s Big Ugly Bill** —a bill that would also strip $2.7 billion in funding from the Maryland Health Department. I want to explain exactly what happens when that much support is pulled from our state:
* Our hospitals are already facing a workforce crisis, and **when hundreds of thousands of Marylanders lose Medicaid coverage, they’ll be forced to use the emergency room for basic needs.** It floods our hospitals and will push our already struggling system to the breaking point.
* Many community health centers, the backbone of care in our neighborhoods, rely on Medicaid to keep their doors open. **Without funding, the very clinics so many rely on for check-ups and health screenings are at risk of closing. **

This bill, passed by the extreme wing of the GOP, has fundamentally changed the rules of our healthcare system. **By forcing more frequent re-enrollment and implementing new, rigid requirements, they’ve created a system designed to let people fall through the cracks. ** The proponents of this bill spend a lot of time calling it “beautiful.” But for the families in Maryland who are now wondering if they'll be able to afford their medication or see a doctor when they need one, there is nothing beautiful about it. We won’t solve these challenges with one massive bill. We solve them through the hard work I started on my very first day on the House Floor: protecting the Affordable Care Act, capping prescription prices, and ensuring our veterans are extended the care they’ve earned. Congresswoman Sarah Elfreth broke barriers in 2024, becoming the youngest woman ever elected to Congress from Maryland. She went to Congress with one thing in mind: delivering for Maryland families on the issues that matter most. Whether it's standing up for federal workers, supporting veterans, protecting the Chesapeake Bay, or tackling the affordability crisis head-on, Sarah is on the front lines, fighting for what is right. And Sarah has delivered on her promises. She has spent her first year in the House advocating for the Third District, successfully passing five bills into law, solving over 1,000 constituent cases, and bringing tens of millions in funding back to her community. She learned her work ethic and tenacity from growing up in a union household and honed her skills of problem-solving and collaborating over six years in the Maryland State Senate. Sarah lives in Annapolis with her fiancé, Eric, and their dog, Ollie. clean_body: 190,000 Marylanders are about to lose their healthcare. | | | Friend, Welcome to the latest edition of Sarah Explains It All. My goal for this series is to cut through the political spin and give you the unvarnished facts about how policy in Washington is actually impacting our lives. Today, we need to talk about a single, sobering number: 190,000 A new analysis revealed that as many as 190,000 Marylanders are at risk of losing their Medicaid coverage under the Trump Administration’s Big Ugly Bill —a bill that would also strip $2.7 billion in funding from the Maryland Health Department. I want to explain exactly what happens when that much support is pulled from our state: Our hospitals are already facing a workforce crisis, and when hundreds of thousands of Marylanders lose Medicaid coverage, they’ll be forced to use the emergency room for basic needs. It floods our hospitals and will push our already struggling system to the breaking point. Many community health centers, the backbone of care in our neighborhoods, rely on Medicaid to keep their doors open. Without funding, the very clinics so many rely on for check-ups and health screenings are at risk of closing. This bill, passed by the extreme wing of the GOP, has fundamentally changed the rules of our healthcare system. By forcing more frequent re-enrollment and implementing new, rigid requirements, they’ve created a system designed to let people fall through the cracks. The proponents of this bill spend a lot of time calling it “beautiful.” But for the families in Maryland who are now wondering if they'll be able to afford their medication or see a doctor when they need one, there is nothing beautiful about it. We won’t solve these challenges with one massive bill. We solve them through the hard work I started on my very first day on the House Floor: protecting the Affordable Care Act, capping prescription prices, and ensuring our veterans are extended the care they’ve earned. = | = The stakes are high, but as I’ve always said: if we focus on the work, we can deliver real results. Onward, Sarah Elfreth | * = | | | ---|---|---|--- Congresswoman Sarah Elfreth broke barriers in 2024, becoming the youngest woman ever elected to Congress from Maryland. She went to Congress with one thing in mind: delivering for Maryland families on the issues that matter most. Whether it's standing up for federal workers, supporting veterans, protecting the Chesapeake Bay, or tackling the affordability crisis head-on, Sarah is on the front lines, fighting for what is right. And Sarah has delivered on her promises. She has spent her first year in the House advocating for the Third District, successfully passing five bills into law, solving over 1,000 constituent cases, and bringing tens of millions in funding back to her community. She learned her work ethic and tenacity from growing up in a union household and honed her skills of problem-solving and collaborating over six years in the Maryland State Senate. Sarah lives in Annapolis with her fiancé, Eric, and their dog, Ollie. To learn more about Sarah, visit: Emails like this are the most effective way to grow our campaign and reach supporters like you. Peter, In October 2021, I had been an employee of Kellogg's for almost 18 years.
I had dropped out of college and started working for the company after my wife got pregnant. Life's easy when all you gotta do is take care of yourself - but we needed diapers and health insurance for our growing family.
Working at Kellogg's used to be a lifelong career. A good-paying job that lets you become a homeowner, live decently, and hopefully retire someday.
But over the years, that changed. Workers were paid less. Cost-of-living adjustments weren't keeping up anywhere near inflation. Retirement and health insurance plans were gutted. It just wasn't right. They were making record profits - and doing it off the backs of workers.
So in October 2021, we walked out. And as president of our local union, I led the strike.
---

Most of us had never walked a picket line. It was cold, but we were determined to hold our lines through the dead of winter if we had to. We were a part of something bigger than ourselves. We were in a fight for the future of the American middle class.
After 11 weeks in the cold, we reached an agreement. More importantly, we saved 500 good-paying union jobs.
It was one of the proudest moments of my life.

Following the strike, I was fired. Someone had to pay - and as union president, my head was on the chopping block.
It's easy to let yourself get beaten down by life. To let big corporations and the politicians they own in Washington make all the decisions - and just accept that that's how things will always be. But that's not me.
Instead, I decided last year to run against one of the most corporate politicians - U.S. Senator Republican Deb Fischer - and we nearly won. I got 47% of the vote in one of the closest Senate races in the country.
Now, I'm running again for the U.S. Senate - this time against billionaire Republican Pete Ricketts - and the first poll shows us virtually TIED: 46% to 45%.
I am taking on a literal billionaire senator. We can finish what we started last year and flip Nebraska's Senate seat for working-class people, but I need grassroots donors like you to give now if we're going to win.

clean_body: Someone had to pay – and as union president, my head was on the chopping block. | | | | | == | == Peter, In October 2021, I had been an employee of Kellogg's for almost 18 years. I had dropped out of college and started working for the company after my wife got pregnant. Life's easy when all you gotta do is take care of yourself - but we needed diapers and health insurance for our growing family. Working at Kellogg's used to be a lifelong career. A good-paying job that lets you become a homeowner, live decently, and hopefully retire someday. But over the years, that changed. Workers were paid less. Cost-of-living adjustments weren't keeping up anywhere near inflation. Retirement and health insurance plans were gutted. It just wasn't right. They were making record profits - and doing it off the backs of workers. So in October 2021, we walked out. And as president of our local union, I led the strike. | == Most of us had never walked a picket line. It was cold, but we were determined to hold our lines through the dead of winter if we had to. We were a part of something bigger than ourselves. We were in a fight for the future of the American middle class. After 11 weeks in the cold, we reached an agreement. More importantly, we saved 500 good-paying union jobs. It was one of the proudest moments of my life. | == Following the strike, I was fired. Someone had to pay - and as union president, my head was on the chopping block. It's easy to let yourself get beaten down by life. To let big corporations and the politicians they own in Washington make all the decisions - and just accept that that's how things will always be. But that's not me. Instead, I decided last year to run against one of the most corporate politicians - U.S. Senator Republican Deb Fischer - and we nearly won. I got 47% of the vote in one of the closest Senate races in the country. Now, I'm running again for the U.S. Senate - this time against billionaire Republican Pete Ricketts - and the first poll shows us virtually TIED: 46% to 45%. I am taking on a literal billionaire senator. We can finish what we started last year and flip Nebraska's Senate seat for working-class people, but I need grassroots donors like you to give now if we're going to win. == | | == | | == | | == | | == | | == | | == | == | I believe we can win this race and keep up the fight for the American middle class. But I'm counting on your support now to win. clean_body: | | | | | Dear Friend, The swamp keeps hoping conservatives will get tired or settle for half-measures.But the stories we’re highlighting this week show exactly the opposite: your State Freedom Caucuses are still pressing forward and making it harder for the swamp to operate in the dark. With so many “Republicans” operating like Democrats in red states, our caucuses are more important than ever–particularly when it comes to exposing bad policy and preserving liberty in an age when both sides are caught up in crony politics. And when elites in our nation’s Capitol fail to act, our members don’t get phased: they continue carrying the torch for liberty in their respective states. Here are the latest examples: | D.C.’S FAILURES UNDERSCORE IMPORTANCE OF STATES The vote against Senator John Kennedy’s effort to include SAVE America Act provisions in reconciliation this week was a setback, but not a sign that election integrity is a low priority for conservatives. Secure elections are foundational to our republic and should be treated like the serious national priority they are. That is exactly why the State Freedom Caucus Network matters so much. While too many Senate Republicans are willing to stand idle, our state caucuses have been moving the ball forward on election integrity in real, concrete ways. The bigger point is this: when the elites in Washington won’t act, the states still can, like** And that is where the network has been critical—building pressure and helping conservative lawmakers turn talking points into actual policy wins. | MISSOURI FREEDOM CAUCUS SECURES BUDGET WINS In Missouri, the Missouri Freedom Caucus is once again making it clear that bad process and bad policy will not go unchallenged. The result? An historic $4.11 BILLION in state budget cuts! The latest fight to secure budget cuts in Missouri underscores a familiar problem in state capitols: leadership wants quiet and easy votes. Freedom Caucus members want accountability and conservative results. They’re willing to work for them, which is exactly what happened. That distinction matters. When our members step up to the plate, they create the pressure needed to stop weak deals before they become law. And they secure actual wins for the people who elected them. | QUICK HITS ️⚡️**Montana — The Montana Freedom Caucus is another example of blatant judicial overreach after liberal justices rewrote the law in Montana, despite the will of the people. Their statement is another reminder that conservatives have to stay loud if they want to stop the machine. ️️⚡️South Carolina — Rep. Adam Morgan of the South Carolina Freedom Caucus continues to pressure the ruling political establishment and plainly about the influence conservatives have in the state, despite leadership’s willingness to recognize it. ️️⚡️Illinois — Other groups are now taking notice of the Illinois Freedom Caucus’ leadership taxpayers from the crony Mega Projects bill. When our members stand firm, people pay attention and the narrative starts to shift. ️️⚡️Louisiana — The Louisiana Freedom Caucus won its first round against an anti-private property rights bill, an important early victory for liberty and for the people who work, own, and build in Louisiana. | RADIO CLIP OF THE WEEK This week’s radio clip features Rep. Drew Roach of the Minnesota Freedom Caucus explaining why he and his colleagues filed articles of impeachment against Governor Tim Walz and Attorney General Keith Ellison for their corruption. It is a strong example of what the network is built to do: equip state lawmakers to hold bad actors accountable when the political establishment would rather look the other way.Watch the clip below. 🎧 Subscribe on (or on your preferred podcast platform)📣 Follow us on X \- 🎵 Follow us on TikTok \- 👍 Follow us on Facebook \- | WE NEED YOUR HELP TO KEEP THE MOMENTUM This week’s highlights are a powerful example of why the State Freedom Caucus Network matters, but they’re far from the only ones. Across the country, our caucuses are pushing back on wasteful spending, defending property rights, and fighting for accountability — even when Republican leadership would rather move on and call it a day. That is what makes this network so important. It gives lawmakers the strategy and backing they need to keep pressing forward, keep the pressure on, and keep turning conservative priorities into real action in the states. We'll be back with another update soon. Until then, please be sure to our efforts so that we can support our State Freedom Caucuses!In Liberty, Andy RothPresidentState Freedom Caucus Network | |

Earlier this week, I was proud to share with you that #LahmeyerForCongress received the OFFICIAL endorsement from the Oklahoma Republican Party Chairw
